description: Wall Street to bread lines — the 1929 crash, Hoovervilles and the limits of Hoover's response.
content_html:
The Wall Street Crash

On 24 October 1929 — Black Thursday — the New York Stock Exchange experienced catastrophic selling as investors tried to offload shares whose prices had been inflated far beyond the value of the underlying companies. A temporary rally followed when leading bankers pooled resources to buy shares and stabilise the market. It did not hold. On Tuesday 29 October — Black Tuesday — share prices collapsed entirely. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost around a quarter of its value in two days. By July 1932, it had fallen 89 per cent from its 1929 peak. It would not recover to pre-crash levels until 1954.

Key Fact

The crash was not caused by a single shock; it reflected structural weaknesses that had been building throughout the 1920s. Share speculation on buying on margin meant millions of investors owed money they could not repay when prices fell. Over-production in agriculture and industry meant companies were already earning less than their inflated share prices suggested. And consumer debt — the hire-purchase economy — left American families without the savings to sustain spending through a downturn.

The Great Depression: Scale and Human Cost

The Crash triggered a cascading economic crisis. Banks that had lent money for share speculation began to fail as borrowers defaulted. Between 1930 and 1933, roughly 9,000 American banks collapsed, wiping out the savings of millions of depositors. Without savings, families cut spending. Businesses responded by cutting production and sacking workers. Unemployment rose from around 3 per cent in 1929 to a peak of approximately 25 per cent by 1932 — around 13 to 15 million people out of work.

The human consequences were visible everywhere. Hoovervilles — shantytowns built from scrap wood, corrugated iron, and cardboard — appeared on the edges of cities and in parks. Bread lines and soup kitchens, many operated by charities and churches, fed hundreds of thousands. The Dust Bowl conditions in the Great Plains from the early 1930s drove hundreds of thousands of farming families off the land, the so-called “Okies” heading to California in search of work.

In June 1930, Hoover signed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff, raising taxes on over 20,000 imported goods to the highest levels in American history. The aim was to protect American industry and farmers from foreign competition. The result was a retaliatory tariff war: countries that exported to the US raised their own barriers, and American exports collapsed. World trade shrank by around 65 per cent between 1929 and 1934. The tariff is widely regarded by economic historians as having significantly deepened and prolonged the Depression.

Hoover’s Response: Neither Nothing Nor Enough

A common misconception among students is that Hoover “did nothing” in the face of the Depression. This is inaccurate, and examiners penalise oversimplification. Hoover did intervene: he convened conferences with business leaders and urged them voluntarily to maintain wages; he increased federal public works spending; and he created the RFC. But his interventions were constrained by his ideological commitment to voluntary co-operation and his deep reluctance to make the federal government directly responsible for individual welfare. At a time when 25 per cent unemployment required emergency action, ideological restraint proved catastrophic for millions of Americans and for Hoover’s presidency.

Key Fact

Hoover’s most significant economic intervention was the creation of the RFC (Reconstruction Finance Corporation) in January 1932, which lent money to banks and businesses at risk of failure. He also increased federal public works spending and encouraged states to create their own relief programmes. But he refused to authorise direct federal relief to unemployed individuals, believing this would create dependency and undermine personal character — a position that seemed increasingly out of touch as unemployment reached 25 per cent.

In July 1932, around 17,000 veterans of the First World War — the “Bonus Army” — marched on Washington DC demanding early payment of a war bonus Congress had promised for 1945. Hoover refused. When a confrontation with police resulted in deaths, he authorised General Douglas MacArthur to disperse the veterans. MacArthur exceeded his orders, using cavalry, tanks, and tear gas to drive the marchers, their wives, and children from their camps. Images of army units attacking their own veterans destroyed what remained of Hoover’s political standing. In November 1932, Franklin D. Roosevelt defeated Hoover in a landslide, winning 42 of 48 states. The Democratic era of American politics had begun.
exam_tip_html: Examiners consistently report that students describe Hoover as doing “nothing” about the Depression. This loses marks. You must show nuance: Hoover did act (RFC, public works, voluntary co-operation schemes), but his actions were inadequate because his ideology prevented him from authorising direct federal relief to individuals, and the Smoot-Hawley Tariff actively worsened the situation. The Bonus Army’s dispersal is an excellent piece of evidence for Hoover’s political failure. Always be specific about dates: the Crash is October 1929, peak unemployment was around 1932, and the election that ended Hoover’s presidency was November 1932.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 (Black Thursday 24th, Black Tuesday 29th) was the trigger for the Great Depression — but its underlying causes lay in share speculation on margin, over-production, and consumer debt from the 1920s boom.
  • By 1932 unemployment had reached approximately 25 per cent; Hoovervilles, bread lines, and the Dust Bowl migration showed the human scale of the crisis.
  • Hoover did intervene (RFC, public works) but refused direct federal relief to individuals; the dispersal of the Bonus Army and the 1932 landslide election loss to Roosevelt sealed his political failure.

practice_questions.text: Outline two features of the Wall Street Crash of October 1929.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Each feature scores 1 mark for identification and 1 additional mark for specific supporting detail. Example features: catastrophic fall in share prices (1), with the Dow Jones losing around a quarter of its value in two days and falling 89 per cent by July 1932 (1); mass selling triggered by share speculation on margin (1), meaning investors who had borrowed to buy shares could not repay their brokers when prices fell, forcing further selling (1). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Great Depression was so severe in the United States.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both reasons fully explained with specific evidence (e.g. the banking crisis saw around 9,000 banks fail between 1930 and 1933, wiping out savings and cutting credit to businesses and families; the Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930 triggered retaliatory tariffs that caused world trade to shrink by about 65 per cent, meaning US exports collapsed at precisely the moment the economy needed demand). Secure: Both reasons explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One explained well, one identified only. Emerging: One or both identified without causal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Hoover's response to the Great Depression is described as 'too little, too late'.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains the ideological constraint (voluntary co-operation, refusal of direct federal relief) as well as specific policy failures (Smoot-Hawley made things worse; RFC was too small and too focused on businesses rather than unemployed individuals); uses the Bonus Army dispersal and the 1932 election result as evidence of political failure. Secure: Two or more factors explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One factor explained, others named. Emerging: General statement without specific evidence.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Hoovervilles during the Great Depression.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature identified, plus 1 mark per supporting detail. Feature 1: Hoovervilles were shantytowns built by homeless and unemployed Americans (1); they were constructed from whatever materials could be found — scrap wood, cardboard, corrugated iron — and appeared on the edges of cities and in parks across the country (1). Feature 2: The name ‘Hooverville’ was a deliberate political statement blaming President Hoover for the crisis (1); their widespread visibility in cities was deeply damaging to Hoover’s reputation as an efficient administrator (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that Hoover's policies made the Great Depression worse? Use your knowledge and any interpretations you have studied to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that acknowledges Hoover’s active interventions (RFC, public works) while arguing his ideological constraints (voluntary co-operation, refusal of direct relief) and policy mistakes (Smoot-Hawley) made the Depression significantly worse; uses specific evidence and engages with at least one interpretation. Secure: Clear argument with evidence across multiple policy areas. Developing: Some awareness of both actions and failures with basic evidence. Emerging: Descriptive account without structured argument. SPaG: 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Compare the following two interpretations of Hoover's presidency during the Depression. Interpretation A argues he was a victim of circumstances beyond any president's control. Interpretation B argues his rigid ideology and policy mistakes significantly deepened the crisis. How far do the interpretations differ, and what might explain their differences?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies key differences (structural vs. individual blame, role of ideology, evidence base); uses own knowledge to evaluate both (global scale of Depression, bank failures for A; Smoot-Hawley, refusal of direct relief, Bonus Army for B); explains why interpretations differ (political perspective, hindsight, evidence available). Secure: Explains differences with relevant own knowledge. Developing: Identifies some differences and supports one. Emerging: Summarises each without explaining differences.

knowledge_checks.q: What name was given to 29 October 1929, the day share prices fully collapsed on the New York Stock Exchange?
What was the Reconstruction Finance Corporation (RFC), created in January 1932?
options: A programme giving food vouchers to unemployed families
A body lending money to banks and businesses to prevent collapses
A public works scheme employing millions

knowledge_checks.q: By 1932, unemployment in the USA had reached approximately _____ per cent.
Shantytowns built by homeless Americans during the Depression were sarcastically named _____ to blame the president.
Match each Depression-era event to the correct date.

flashcard_questions.q: What were Black Thursday and Black Tuesday?
flashcard_questions.a: 24 and 29 October 1929 — the two days of catastrophic share price falls that triggered the Great Depression
Buying shares with borrowed money — when prices fell, investors couldn't repay loans, forcing panic selling
A law raising tariffs on over 20,000 imported goods; triggered retaliatory tariffs and shrunk world trade by ~65%
A shantytown built by homeless and unemployed Americans, sarcastically named to blame Hoover
Around 17,000 First World War veterans who marched on Washington demanding early payment of their war bonus

flashcard_questions.q: How was the Bonus Army dispersed, and why did it damage Hoover?
flashcard_questions.a: MacArthur used cavalry, tanks, and tear gas — images of soldiers attacking veterans wrecked Hoover's reputation
Hoover's Reconstruction Finance Corporation — lent money to failing banks and businesses

flashcard_questions.q: Why did Hoover refuse direct federal relief to individuals?
flashcard_questions.a: He believed it would create dependency and undermine personal character — his 'voluntary co-operation' ideology

flashcard_questions.q: What was the result of the 1932 presidential election?
flashcard_questions.a: Franklin D. Roosevelt defeated Hoover in a landslide, winning 42 of 48 states

glossary_terms.definition: 24 October 1929, the first day of catastrophic selling on the New York Stock Exchange, when share prices collapsed and panic spread through the financial system.
Buying shares using borrowed money from a broker, meaning that when prices fell, investors could not repay their loans and mass selling ensued.
Shantytowns built by homeless and unemployed Americans during the Great Depression, sarcastically named after President Hoover to blame him for the crisis.
A 1930 tariff that raised taxes on over 20,000 imported goods to record levels, intended to protect American industry but which triggered retaliatory tariffs and shrank world trade.
Hoover's belief that voluntary co-operation between businesses, communities, and individuals — rather than direct federal government spending — was the proper response to economic crisis.
The Reconstruction Finance Corporation, established by Hoover in January 1932, which lent money to banks, railroads, and businesses to prevent further collapses.
